summary: Describes how to use OSPF-MDR (from RFC 5614) in a single-hop broadcast network, a special case of an ad hoc network where every router is a direct neighbor of every other. It includes configuration advice and simplified mechanisms. This is an experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: When everyone is in one small room and hears everyone, the route-sharing rules can be simpler. This explains how.

questions: using ospf mdr on broadcast network
how to use ospf-mdr on a broadcast network
subtitle: How to run OSPF-MDR on a network where every router can hear every other, with recommended settings and simpler algorithms.

tldr.problem: OSPF-MDR was designed for mobile ad hoc networks, but a single-hop broadcast network, where every router is a one-hop neighbor of every other, still needs different costs per neighbor that an OSPF broadcast interface cannot express.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends parameter settings for OSPF-MDR in this case and gives two optional simplifications: an alternative way to pick which neighbors go in the router-LSA, and a simpler MDR selection algorithm.
tldr.outcome: The simplifications are interoperable with the full procedures but MUST NOT be used if two routers could be more than one hop apart. The RFC is Experimental and updates RFC 5614.

today: RFC 7038 is an Experimental document that updates RFC 5614, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: OSPF-MDR on a Single-Hop Network
sections.content:
OSPF-MDR (RFC 5614) extends OSPF for mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) through a new interface type. It replaces the Designated Router with a connected dominating set of MANET Designated Routers (MDRs) and the Backup Designated Router with Backup MDRs (BMDRs). MDRs take primary responsibility for flooding link state advertisements and keep the number of adjacencies low.

This document covers a single-hop broadcast network, a special case of a MANET in which every router is a one-hop neighbor of every other. Unlike an OSPF broadcast interface, such an interface can have a different cost for each neighbor. The text gives the example of a radio system that does layer-2 routing and so has a different number of layer-2 hops to different layer-3 neighbors. The document shows how OSPF-MDR can reach the same goals as the OSPF Hybrid Broadcast and Point-to-Multipoint interface type (RFC 6845). An understanding of RFC 5614 is assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a class picks one leader to pass messages. Here everyone is in the same small room, but each person is a different distance away, so each gets their own distance number.

sections.title: Recommended Settings and Results
sections.content:
For this setting, AdjConnectivity SHOULD be 2 (biconnected), which gives the smoothest handover when one router replaces another as MDR. It MAY be 1 (uniconnected), with a slightly less smooth handover, and SHOULD NOT be 0 (full topology), since that needs adjacencies between all pairs of routers. An adjacency SHOULD be eliminated if neither router is an MDR or BMDR.

LSAFullness MUST be 4 or 5 if full-topology LSAs are needed, and MAY be 1 (min-cost LSAs) otherwise, which reduces the advertised links while still giving shortest paths.

With AdjConnectivity 1 or 2 and full-topology LSAs, one MDR is selected and becomes adjacent with every other router, as in an OSPF broadcast network. Two BMDRs are also selected, because the selection algorithm makes the MDR/BMDR backbone biconnected. When all adjacencies are full, each router-LSA lists point-to-point links to all bidirectional neighbors.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick one main leader and two helpers so that if the leader steps out, messages still get through. Do not make every pair of people shake hands, because that wastes time.

sections.title: An Alternative Way to Originate Router-LSAs
sections.content:
With LSAFullness 4, a router lists point-to-point links for all fully adjacent neighbors and for all bidirectional neighbors that are routable. This section defines an optional alternative, LSAFullness 5, that avoids checking whether a neighbor is routable. It is interoperable with the other LSAFullness choices.

The MDR lists a link for each fully adjacent neighbor, and it becomes adjacent with all of its neighbors. Each non-MDR router lists a link for each fully adjacent neighbor and, if it is fully adjacent with the MDR, for each bidirectional neighbor that the MDR's router-LSA includes.

The reason it works: OSPF's SPF calculation lets router i use router j as a next hop only if j advertises a link back. So two non-MDR routers must both advertise each other before they can use each other, which means a path of fully adjacent links through the MDR must exist in both directions first.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kids may only pass notes directly once both have written the other's name on their lists. Using the leader's list as a guide makes sure that only happens when the leader can reach both.

sections.title: A Simplified MDR Selection Algorithm
sections.content:
The full MDR selection algorithm simplifies for single-hop networks. The result is like the OSPF DR election, but with two Backup MDRs, and it is interoperable with the full algorithm. Routers compare tuples of (RtrPri, MDR Level, RID) in lexicographic order.

Phase 1, building the neighbor connectivity matrix, is not required. In Phase 2 a router with a larger tuple than all its bidirectional neighbors selects itself as MDR. Otherwise an MDR demotes itself to BMDR before Phase 3. In Phase 3 the router finds the neighbor Rmax with the largest tuple. If two neighbors other than Rmax have a larger tuple than the router, it becomes MDR Other. If not, it becomes a BMDR.

In Phase 4 each router picks a Parent and, if AdjConnectivity is 2, a Backup Parent. A non-MDR router's Parent is the MDR. These are advertised in the DR and Backup DR fields of Hello packets, as in OSPF. The simplified procedures of sections 3 and 4 MUST NOT be used if two routers could be more than one hop apart.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone compares scores. The top scorer is the leader, the next ones are helpers, and the rest just follow the leader.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC states that using OSPF-MDR in a single-hop broadcast network raises no security issues beyond those already covered in RFC 5614. It adds no new security mechanism of its own.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new to worry about here beyond what the main rules already cover.
